title: Why Can You Still Hear Voices with Noise-Cancelling Headphones? | So That's Why
description:
The subway rumble vanishes in an instant, so why can you still hear your coworker talking right next to you? Many people think noise-cancelling headphones are an invisible forcefield that absorbs all sound like a sponge. But the reality is the exact opposite: headphones don't suck up sound—they play a second sound right into your ear!

In this episode, the Chief and Little Q break down the physics behind noise-cancelling headphones:
- Canceling sound with sound? When wave crests meet troughs in "destructive interference"
- When two sounds cancel out, where does the original energy go? The secret of acoustic impedance in the ear canal
- Why do low-frequency rumbles vanish while voices stay? A tolerance battle between wavelengths differing by 20 times
- Where does that "ear pressure" sensation come from when ANC turns on? A sensory illusion from brain contrast
- A 60-microsecond race against time: can headphone chips keep up with the speed of sound?
- Regular periodic waves vs. sudden random voices: why algorithms can't predict the next second
- Why does your own voice sound so loud when talking with headphones on? Bone conduction and the occlusion effect
- How can you test your headphones' noise cancellation limit at home in one second?

The illustrations in this episode were generated with AI. The devices shown are generic representations. All numerical values come from acoustics textbooks and engineering literature.

Data current as of 2026-11-14

p001.text: Chief! These new headphones are amazing!

p002.text: The subway rumble just completely vanished,

p003.text: but you're talking right next to me,

p004.text: so why can I still hear you loud and clear?

p005.text: A lot of people think noise-cancelling headphones are an invisible forcefield,

p006.text: absorbing every sound like a sponge.

p009.text: it can't stop deep bass waves!

p010.text: Subway track rumbles and AC hums,

p011.text: slip straight through cushion gaps into your ear.

p012.text: Pores absorb sharp highs by friction,

p013.text: but long bass waves go right in!

p016.text: The real secret isn't absorbing sound,

p017.text: it's that the headphones play a second sound right into your ear!

p019.text: Wouldn't that make things even louder?

p023.text: How does sound cancel out another sound?

p025.text: Sound is air being pushed and pulled in waves.

p026.text: Compressed air makes a high-pressure crest;

p027.text: stretched air makes a low-pressure trough.

p028.text: That push and pull lets eardrums hear!

p029.text: How do you flatten that out?

p030.text: The mic detects the incoming noise wave,

p031.text: and the chip computes an anti-phase wave!

p032.text: An outside crest meets an earbud trough;

p033.text: high plus low pressure zeroes out at the eardrum!

p036.text: In the tiny ear canal, pressures cancel out,

p037.text: so the eardrum stills, and all goes quiet.

p039.text: where does the original energy go?

p040.text: Sharp question! Energy never just vanishes:

p041.text: anti-phase shifts ear canal acoustic impedance!

p042.text: Opposing pushes stop outside noise from doing work,

p043.text: choking sound energy at the ear canal's source!

p045.text: was it invented only with new chips?

p046.text: A German engineer tried it ninety years ago,

p047.text: but without computers, math was too slow!

p048.text: In 1936, Paul Lueg patented a tube test,

p049.text: but tubes were too slow, making noise louder.

p050.text: Only with modern digital processing chips

p051.text: could active noise cancelling fit inside.

p053.text: why only cut trains, not your voice?

p055.text: Bass and treble waves differ by dozens!

p057.text: A 2,000 Hz voice wave is just 17 cm.

p058.text: Over three meters is longer than a bed!

p059.text: So what does wavelength have to do with whether it can be cancelled?

p060.text: Your ear canal is only 2 centimeters!

p061.text: A 3-meter wave rolls in, keeping canal pressure even.

p062.text: The anti-phase wave from the speaker easily blankets the whole canal,

p063.text: creating what acoustics calls a 'zone of quiet'.

p064.text: Like stepping inside a peaceful little bubble!

p065.text: Then what happens with the short waves of human voices?

p066.text: Voice waves are way too short!

p067.text: Shift one centimeter or lag microseconds,

p071.text: Is that why engineers skip treble?

p072.text: Right! Over 1,000 Hz is a cancellation trap;

p073.text: forcing it just creates piercing howls.

p074.text: What if I turn, or buds tilt slightly?

p075.text: A half-centimeter shift throws treble anti-phase off!

p076.text: Crests that should cancel stack right on top of crests!

p077.text: No wonder! But why do my ears always feel that stuffy pressure

p078.text: right when I turn on noise cancellation?

p080.text: When bass hums vanish, the brain tricks your senses!

p081.text: Your brain thinks you're dropping in an elevator;

p082.text: breathe deep for two minutes, and it fades away.

p084.text: yet know if your ear canal is quiet?

p085.text: Dual mics team up inside the buds!

p086.text: One hears outside; one guards your eardrum inside.

p088.text: while the inside mic tweaks leaks live.

p089.text: Since the inside mic sits right next to the ear,

p090.text: why can't it just handle everything on its own?

p091.text: Because the inside mic has a fatal time delay!

p092.text: It only notices sound once it's already in your ear—if playback is late, it howls!

p093.text: Like pointing a mic at karaoke speakers;

p094.text: so the inside mic only handles sounds under 500 Hz.

p096.text: Can't it outrun sound in the air?

p099.text: Mic pickup, chip math, and speaker pulses

p100.text: take at least 20 microseconds on fast chips!

p102.text: How does it catch subway noise?

p104.text: Repeating by millisecond, chips predict ahead!

p105.text: Knowing the rhythm, chips prep anti-phase waves in advance;

p106.text: but human speech is totally random!

p107.text: No one can guess if a 'p' or 't' comes next;

p108.text: chips can't guess, and sounds enter before math is done!

p109.text: Makes sense! Subway rails roll with steady rhythms,

p110.text: while people jump in randomly to chat!

p111.text: Right! Regular waves can be predicted, random ones cannot;

p112.text: that's the clever math behind noise cancelling.

p113.text: What about transparency mode on earbuds?

p114.text: How does that let voices through?

p115.text: It's opposite! The outside mic grabs human voices,

p116.text: timing it right to play straight to eardrums, like clear headphones!

p117.text: So the secret of the whole headphone

p118.text: is really a precise dance between physics and math?

p120.text: First: long bass waves give big leeway!

p122.text: While choppy human voices can't be guessed ahead!

p123.text: Spot on! Little Q gets top marks for cracking the case!

p124.text: High voice pitches are blocked physically by thick ear cushions.

p125.text: Foam and outer shells follow acoustic mass laws,

p126.text: cutting voices over 2,000 Hz by ten-plus decibels.

p127.text: So with ANC on in an office,

p128.text: AC hums vanish, yet you hear your name called!

p129.text: No wonder! And when I talk with headphones on,

p130.text: my own voice sounds super loud and clear too!

p131.text: Bone conduction! Vocal cords vibrate your skull,

p132.text: sending sound into your inner ear without canal air!

p133.text: Even if earbuds sucked out all canal air,

p134.text: bone sound still vibrates your cochlea!

p135.text: True! If I plug my ears and hum,

p136.text: it buzzes louder inside my head!

p138.text: Sealed canals trap bone vibrations, making sounds deeper.

p139.text: How can we test our headphones' limits

p141.text: Easy! Put on buds with ANC on, and snap fingers or tap keyboards!

p142.text: Crisp high clicks stay, while fan rumbles underneath vanish.

p144.text: the teamwork of passive and active ANC!

p145.text: Leaving voices slightly audible protects safety too.

p146.text: Imagine walking outside without hearing shouts or horns!

p147.text: Leaving a little outside sound in

p148.text: keeps you from getting startled by coworkers or traffic!
